name: The shore cottonwood grove at Sixteenth to Eighteenth Street

existence.note: A RECOLLECTION, GRADED AS ONE. Robert G. Clarke, 1890, of his childhood on the Clark farm: 'This was one of a grove, consisting of perhaps fifty to seventy-five large cottonwoods, extending from a little north of Sixteenth to a little south of Eighteenth Street. Almost in the center of this grove ... stood a "clump" of eight or nine trees.' What he describes is the late 1830s and 1840s; Mary Clark Williams's 'large and thrifty tree' about 1835 and Arnold's 'some cottonwood trees' of 1836 carry it back to this scene. No picture of the grove is in this corpus, so its existence is inferred, not attested.

research_note: WHY z05 AND NOT z08: z08_lakeshore's cottonwood is the 5-15 m dune form; Clarke's are 'large', and z05_riverbank_timber's 22-30 m populus_deltoides is the only record of the full-grown tree. WHAT IS INVENTED is every position except the clump's centre, and the strip's depth (docs/LIBERTIES.md L-shore-grove-1835-2766). WHAT WOULD MOVE THESE: Andreas's engraving of the 18th Street tree (vol. 1, p. 31), an early plat of the Clark farm or of Eighteenth Street that draws trees, or a photograph of the shore before the Illinois Central's fill.
